intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-11 (HMND11) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPTAN1 gene, which encodes alpha-II spectrin.

checks.claim: Autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-11 (HMND11) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the SPTAN1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We identified patients with heterozygous nonsense mutations in the αII-spectrin gene, SPTAN1, in three separate dominant hereditary motor neuropathy families via next-generation sequencing.
checks.explanation: Heterozygous SPTAN1 mutations in dominant HMN families; HMND11 designation is OMIM nomenclature.

checks.claim: The SPTAN1 gene encodes alpha-II spectrin.
checks.evidence_quote: heterozygous nonsense mutations in the αII-spectrin gene, SPTAN1
checks.explanation: SPTAN1 identified as the alpha-II spectrin gene.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal dominant distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-11 (HMND11) is a juvenile-onset form of distal hereditary motor neuropathy. Distal hereditary motor neuropathies are a rare subgroup of inherited peripheral neuropathies characterized by length-dependent axonal degeneration of lower motor neurons without significant involvement of sensory neurons. In HMND11, penetrance can be variable and severity differs greatly between patients (Beijer et al., 2019).

paragraphs.text: Beijer et al. (2019) reported 3 unrelated families with autosomal dominant juvenile-onset hereditary motor neuropathy. Affected individuals had a length-dependent axonal degeneration of lower motor neurons without significant involvement of sensory neurons. Penetrance was variable in 2 of the 3 families, and phenotype severity differed greatly between patients.

Dong et al. (2021) reported a de novo SPTAN1 nonsense mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary motor neuropathy.

paragraphs.text: Beijer et al. (2019) used next-generation sequencing in 3 unrelated families with autosomal dominant juvenile-onset hereditary motor neuropathy and found heterozygous nonsense mutations in the SPTAN1 gene. Mutant mRNA with the nonsense mutations was degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, and protein levels were reduced in patient cells. They noted that dominant-negative SPTAN1 mutations had already been described as causing a range of epilepsy phenotypes.

paragraphs.text: Ylikallio et al. (2020) identified a de novo SPTAN1 mutation in a patient with axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and a developmental disorder. The patient was a 16-year-old male with a frameshift variant in SPTAN1. In addition to peripheral neuropathy, he had severe dyslexia and difficulties with executive function.

checks.claim: The patient with a de novo SPTAN1 mutation reported by Ylikallio et al. (2020) was a 16-year-old male.
checks.evidence_quote: Neuropsychological findings were generally consistent with those identified in a study by Ylikallio et al. [7] [*] involving a 16-year-old male with a frameshift variant in SPTAN1.
checks.explanation: Second-hand: the evidence is a paragraph of Luongo-Zink et al. (2022) (PMID 35620303) describing PMID 33206935, not the paper's own text; the claim was not checked against PMID 33206935 itself. Verdict on the later paper's description: supported. Supported only by a later paper's description (Luongo-Zink et al., 2022), not by the paper's own text, which was not supplied.

Only a later paper (Liu et al., 2023) says this, and it refers to 'patients with SPTAN1 mutations' in general rather than to this particular patient.

Only a later paper (Liu et al., 2023) says this, and it does not tie the finding to this patient. Luongo-Zink et al.
